items_missed: No 'How are you today?', no agenda statement, no 'sound good?' confirmation
Never asked about packing needs or box count — leaned entirely on last year's profile
Never asked about additional stops, access/parking/HOA, or destination stairs/floors
Never asked the moving-stressors question ('anything you're particularly worried about?')
Pricing was a bare number — quoted $204/hr with no 'pricing is super simple' framing and no list of what's included (gas, truck, taxes, insurance, wrap, pads, bands, tools)
No On-Time Guarantee — gave the 8:30-9:00 window with no discount promise attached
Entire Clock section skipped — no on-site start, no 2.5-hour minimum, no 15-minute increments, no sense-check
Entire Save Your Ass speech skipped — no prep-shortens-the-move framing, no consolidation examples, no carload tip
Never asked 'any other questions before I let you go?' — the customer had to ask 'is there anything else I need to do?' himself after Dustin had already started wrapping up
No BOLDED email detail list, no 'reply with any corrections', no hours or how to reach us

Told the customer that profile fields 'don't really matter like the bedrooms or the house you're moving into' — undercuts the intake process and gives the customer a reason to think the estimate is loose
top_strength: Efficient use of the repeat-customer history — he pulled up the prior Einstein move, used it as a live reference point ('two guys five hours'), and caught a stale drive-time value in the system (30 min showing, actually 11 min after refresh) rather than letting a bad number sit in the estimate.
coaching_note: This was a five-minute order-take on a warm repeat customer — easy to book, but zero differentiators landed. The single highest-value change is the Save Your Ass prep speech: it's the one section that actually moves estimate accuracy, and on a 2,200 sqft three-bedroom it was worth more than everything else he skipped. Also stop telling customers parts of the profile 'don't really matter.'
phone_presence_notes: Warm and upbeat throughout with steady affirmations ('awesome', 'sweet', 'I appreciate you') and the customer matched the energy ('Awesome, love it'), held back only by barely using Drake's name.
